summary: Turborepo is a Rust build system for JavaScript monorepos. The tool itself is a workspace of about twenty crates, with turborepo-lib holding the run pipeline, task graph and hashing. Around it sit npm-published JavaScript packages, a documentation site, and four large fixture directories: examples, integration tests, lockfile fixtures and template apps.

districts.name: The Foundry
districts.purpose: The Rust workspace: CLI shim, run pipeline, task engine, caching, source control integration, daemon and terminal UI.

districts.name: The Distributors
districts.purpose: Everything published to npm around the binary: create-turbo, codemods, generators, the ESLint plugin and the telemetry client.

districts.name: The Showrooms
districts.purpose: Runnable starter monorepos, one per ecosystem, kept building so create-turbo always produces a working workspace.

districts.name: Proving Grounds
districts.purpose: End-to-end integration suites that run the real binary against generated monorepos.

districts.name: The Archives
districts.purpose: Recorded lockfiles from every supported package manager, used to check dependency resolution against real files.

districts.name: Knowledge District
districts.purpose: The documentation site and the internal factory app that generates repository content.

districts.name: Civic Offices
districts.purpose: Workflows for Rust tests, JS package tests, linting, release gating and refreshing the examples on release.

districts.name: Maintenance Depot
districts.purpose: Repository chores: formatting, version bookkeeping and release helpers invoked by CI.

importantModules.role: The binary entry point; a thin shell that hands straight to turborepo-lib.
One turbo run: resolves scope, builds the task graph, then executes it with caching.
The task dependency graph: what may run, in what order, and what can run in parallel.
Computes the hash that decides a cache hit; the idea the whole tool rests on.
Local and remote cache storage and retrieval for task outputs.
Workspace discovery: finds packages, package managers and the dependency graph between them.
The full command line surface, with snapshot tests pinning the help output.
The background daemon that keeps file watching warm between runs.
Terminal output: the task list, interleaved logs and the interactive run view.
Migrations that rewrite turbo.json and package scripts when the configuration format changes.

strengths: The Rust workspace is cut along real seams: caching, source control, lockfiles, file watching and the daemon are each their own crate.
Correctness is pinned by recorded artefacts rather than prose: lockfile fixtures for every package manager and snapshot tests for the CLI help.
Every published example is a real workspace that CI refreshes on release, so the getting-started path cannot rot silently.
Breaking configuration changes ship with codemods, so upgrading is a command rather than a manual edit.
Only 13 open issues against a repository of this size suggests the tracker is actively groomed.
concerns: Fixtures dominate the tree: examples, lockfile-tests, turborepo-tests and apps together outweigh the source by several times, so the top level hides where the code is.
turborepo-lib is a catch-all crate holding the CLI, run pipeline, engine and hashing while the surrounding crates stay narrow.
The repository mixes two toolchains, Rust and pnpm JavaScript, so a contributor needs both set up before anything builds.
